--- title: "Multiple Linear Regression" subtitle: "AE 15 review, then more than one predictor" author: "Prof. Eric Friedlander" footer: "[🔗 MATH 2025 - Fall 2026 - Schedule](https://ericfriedlander.github.io/math2025-fa26/)" logo: "../images/logo.png" format: revealjs: theme: slides.scss multiplex: false transition: fade slide-number: false incremental: false chalkboard: true html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" execute: freeze: auto echo: true cache: false knitr: opts_chunk: R.options: width: 200 bibliography: references.bib --- # Review: AE 15 ## Where we are {.smaller} You were asked to finish AE 15 after class. Let's check in on each part: 1. Parts 1-2: $R^2$ for a slope, Cohen's $d$ for a difference in means. 2. Part 3: every group's predictors. 3. Part 4: effect size, sample size, and power. 4. Part 5: reflection. Then we start **multiple** regression. ## Parts 1-2: $R^2$ and $d$ {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} bmi_fit <- lm(sysBP ~ BMI, data = fram) bmi_fit |> glance() |> select(r.squared, p.value) |> kable(digits = 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | r.squared| p.value| |---------:|-------:| | 0.1069| 0| ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dia_fit <- lm(sysBP ~ diabetes_status, data = fram) c(slope_over_sigma = unname(coef(dia_fit)[2] / sigma(dia_fit)), effectsize = cohens_d(sysBP ~ diabetes_status, data = fram)$Cohens_d) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` slope_over_sigma effectsize -0.7072686 0.7072686 ``` ::: ::: ::: question BMI explains about what percent of the variation in `sysBP`? How does that compare to age (about 15%)? Why do the two $d$ values have opposite signs? ::: ## Part 3: everyone's predictors {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Predictor n n in '1' group R² d p-value
totChol 4190 NA 0.044 NA 0.0000
heartRate 4239 NA 0.033 NA 0.0000
glucose 3852 NA 0.020 NA 0.0000
cigsPerDay 4211 NA 0.008 NA 0.0000
currentSmoker 4240 2095 0.017 0.26 0.0000
TenYearCHD 4240 644 0.047 0.62 0.0000
prevalentStroke 4240 25 0.003 0.75 0.0002
BPMeds 4187 124 0.065 1.55 0.0000
````` ::: ::: ::: question Which predictors are **detectable** (p < 0.05)? Which are **meaningful**? ::: ## Part 4: $d$ vs. power {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) sim_sex <- function(n_samp, reps = 300) { map(1:reps, \(i) { fit <- lm(sysBP ~ male, data = resample(fram, n_samp)) tibble(d = coef(fit)[2] / sigma(fit), p = tidy(fit)$p.value[2]) }) |> list_rbind() |> summarize(mean_d = mean(d), power = mean(p < 0.05)) } bind_rows(`n = 100` = sim_sex(100), `n = 4000` = sim_sex(4000), .id = "sample size") |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |sample size | mean_d| power| |:-----------|------:|-----:| |n = 100 | -0.068| 0.060| |n = 4000 | -0.073| 0.623| ::: ::: ::: question What stayed put and what changed as $n$ grew? What does that say about the different jobs of effect size and sample size? ::: ## Part 5: reflection {.smaller} A researcher tests a new teaching method on 12 students and finds p = 0.30. They conclude, "The method has no effect." ::: question What is wrong with this conclusion? How could a power analysis have helped? What if they had tested 12,000 students and found p = 0.001 for a 0.3-point gain on a 100-point exam? ::: . . . - Failing to reject is **not** evidence of no effect: with n = 12, power was probably low. - A power analysis before the study tells you how many students you need for the effect you care about. - With 12,000 students the result is **statistically** significant but probably not **practically** significant. ## From one predictor to many {.smaller} Every model so far has had **one** predictor. But the world is rarely that tidy: - Blood pressure depends on age **and** BMI **and** sex... - Bike rentals depend on temperature **and** the season **and** the weather... Today: **multiple linear regression (MLR)**. # Multiple linear regression ## Data: DC bikeshare {.smaller} Daily rentals from the Capital Bikeshare system in Washington, DC (you saw this in Lectures 3-7). - **Response**: `count`, total bikes rented that day - **Predictors**: `temp_orig` (temperature, °C) and `season` (winter, spring, summer, fall) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 731 Columns: 3 $ count 985, 801, 1349, 1562, 1600, 1606, 1510, 959, 822, 1321, 1263… $ temp_orig 14.110847, 14.902598, 8.050924, 8.200000, 9.305237, 8.378268… $ season winter, winter, winter, winter, winter, winter, winter, wint… ``` ::: ::: ## Recall: two simple models {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} temp_fit <- lm(count ~ temp_orig, data = bikeshare) season_fit <- lm(count ~ season, data = bikeshare) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 1214.64| 161.16| 7.54| 0| |temp_orig | 161.97| 7.44| 21.76| 0| ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 2604.13| 116.60| 22.33| 0| |seasonspring | 2388.20| 164.22| 14.54| 0| |seasonsummer | 3040.17| 163.35| 18.61| 0| |seasonfall | 2124.03| 165.59| 12.83| 0| ::: ::: ::: question Warmer days have more rentals. Summer has more rentals than winter. Are these two findings telling us the **same** thing or **different** things? ::: ## Why use both? {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](17-mlr-intro_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: question Season and temperature are related to each other. If we only use temperature, what is the temperature slope "absorbing"? ::: ## The MLR model {.smaller} **Recall:** the simple linear regression model assumes $$ Y|X\sim N(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X, \sigma_{\epsilon}^2) $$ . . . **Similarly:** the multiple linear regression model assumes $$ Y|X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p \sim N(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots + \beta_p X_p, \sigma_{\epsilon}^2) $$ . . . At any combination of the predictors, the mean response is $$ \mu_{Y|X_1, \ldots, X_p} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1} + \dots + \beta_p X_p \qquad \hat{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_{1} + \dots + \hat{\beta}_p X_{p} $$ ## Fitting the model in R {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mlr_fit <- lm(count ~ temp_orig + season, data = bikeshare) mlr_fit |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 745.79| 187.48| 3.98| 0.00| |temp_orig | 152.23| 12.64| 12.05| 0.00| |seasonspring | 848.72| 197.08| 4.31| 0.00| |seasonsummer | 490.20| 259.01| 1.89| 0.06| |seasonfall | 1342.87| 164.59| 8.16| 0.00| ::: ::: . . . `season` has four levels, so R makes **three** indicator variables (winter is the reference level): $$ \widehat{\text{count}} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \,\text{temp} + \hat{\beta}_2 \,\text{spring} + \hat{\beta}_3 \,\text{summer} + \hat{\beta}_4 \,\text{fall} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: $$ \widehat{\text{count}} = 746 + 152.2 \,\text{temp} + 849 \,\text{spring} + 490 \,\text{summer} + 1343 \,\text{fall} $$ ## What does the model look like? {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](17-mlr-intro_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: question How many lines? How many slopes? How many intercepts? Which coefficient moves a line up or down? ::: ## Interpreting $\hat{\beta}_j$ {.smaller} The coefficient $\hat{\beta}_j$ is the expected change in the **mean** of $y$ when $x_j$ increases by one unit, **holding the values of all other predictors constant**. . . . ::: question Interpret the temperature coefficient in context. Interpret the `summer` coefficient in context. What does the intercept represent, and is it meaningful? ::: . . . Notice that the temperature slope in the MLR is **not** the temperature slope from the simple model: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |model | temp_orig slope| |:--------------------------|---------------:| |count ~ temp_orig | 162.0| |count ~ temp_orig + season | 152.2| ::: ::: ::: question Why did the slope change (a little)? What was the simple model's slope absorbing? ::: ## Activity: Parts 0-3 {.smaller} ::: appex 📋 [AE 17 - Multiple Linear Regression with the Coffee Truck](https://ericfriedlander.github.io/math2025-fa26/ae/ae-17-mlr-coffee-truck.html) ::: - Part 0: load the pre-generated coffee truck data (your group is assigned a categorical variable). - Part 1: explore `Sales`, `Temperature`, and your categorical variable. - Part 2: fit two simple models, then the multiple regression. - Part 3: interpret every coefficient and plot the lines. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: # Prediction ## Prediction {.smaller} ::: question How many bikes do we expect on a 25°C summer day? ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} new_day <- tibble(temp_orig = 25, season = "summer") predict(mlr_fit, new_day) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 5041.681 ``` ::: ::: ## Cautions {.smaller} - **Do not extrapolate!** With several predictors you can extrapolate in many directions at once, even when each predictor is individually in range. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |season | min_temp| max_temp| |:------|--------:|--------:| |winter | 2.4| 23.5| |spring | 10.4| 33.1| |summer | 19.2| 35.3| |fall | 9.1| 27.0| ::: ::: ::: question Would you trust a prediction for a 30°C winter day? ::: . . . - The model shows **association, not causation**. Season and temperature are tangled together in observational data. ## Activity: Part 4 {.smaller} ::: appex 📋 [AE 17 - Multiple Linear Regression with the Coffee Truck](https://ericfriedlander.github.io/math2025-fa26/ae/ae-17-mlr-coffee-truck.html) ::: - Part 4: predict `Sales` for a new day. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Coming next {.smaller} In our plot, all four seasons have the **same** temperature slope (parallel lines). ::: question Is it believable that an extra degree adds the same number of rentals in winter as in summer? ::: . . . Next time: categorical predictors in more depth, and what to do when the slope differs by group. ## Recap {.smaller} - **MLR** models the mean response as a linear function of several predictors. - Each coefficient is the change in mean response per unit change in that predictor, **holding the others constant**. - A coefficient can change when other predictors are added, especially when the predictors are related to each other. - Prediction works as in SLR (`predict()`), but extrapolation can happen in many directions. - An additive model with a categorical predictor gives **parallel lines**: one slope, one intercept per level.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
